paper.title: A guide to estimating the canonical income process in quasidifferences
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference appear in the article. …

registers.role: supplies the earnings histories whose autocovariance structure is matched: both the data on the outcome (residual log earnings) and the sample frame; no treatment variable is taken from a register
variables_mentioned: earnings (log earnings, expressed in 1981 Danish kroner)
share of the year worked as a full-time employee

linkages: no record linkage is described: a single birth cohort (Danish males born in 1952) is followed over 26 years within the administrative earnings records
the simulated data of Tables 1-4 and 6-8 and the PSID age structure used in Section 5.4 are not linked to the Danish data in any way

sample.universe: Danish males born in 1952 with administrative earnings records
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (a balanced panel of individuals with 26 annual earnings observations each)
selection_rules: keep the cohort of males born in 1952, observed during 1981-2006
drop individuals who were ever self-employed
drop records for males working less than 10% of the year as full-time employees
drop earnings histories with growth outliers, defined as an increase of earnings in adjacent periods by more than 500% or a drop by less than -80%
keep a balanced sample (26 earnings observations per individual)
sample.period: 1981-2006 (Section 5.3); the introduction on p. 1233 describes the same application as covering 1984-2008

construction_notes: Earnings are expressed in the 1981 Danish kroner.

Predictable variation in earnings is removed by running, for each year, cross-sectional regressions of log earnings on educational dummies, a third-order polynomial in age, and the interaction of the educational dummies with the age polynomial; the income process is estimated on the residuals.
The sample selection criteria are those of Daly et al. (2022).
For the Danish data the income process allows an MA(1) transitory component and variances of persistent and transitory shocks that vary over time.

Estimation in quasidifferences requires a grid for the persistence: a piecewise linear grid with 100 points ranging from 0.3 to 1.4, split into [0.3,0.5], (0.5,0.7], (0.7,1.1] and (1.1,1.4] with 5, 10, 70 and 15 equidistant points respectively.
Small-sample evidence for the Danish data comes from 100 bootstrap samples of 1000 individuals drawn from the 13,543-individual sample.

The Monte Carlo data of Tables 1-4 are simulated from equation (1) for 100 samples per design with N = 1000 or 10,000, T = 15 or 30, benchmark variances of fixed effects, persistent and transitory shocks of 0.10, 0.01 and 0.04, true persistence 0.90 or 0.995, and either zero initial conditions or var(z_i0) = sigma^2_eta (1 - rho^30)/(1 - rho^2).

The data of Tables 6-8 come from a calibrated standard incomplete-markets lifecycle model (CRRA utility with gamma = 2, 4% interest rate, work from age 26, retirement at 65, death at 90, replacement rate 0.70, discount factor calibrated to a wealth-to-income ratio of 3), simulated for fifteen years per household with the PSID 1978-1992 age distribution and a consumption measurement-error variance of 0.04.
The reported Danish period is inconsistent across the paper: 1981-2006 in Section 5.3 (which matches the 26 earnings observations) versus 1984-2008 in the introduction.

links.pointer_quote: We find that equally weighted estimation often results in downward-biased estimates of the persistence in small and large samples regardless of the magnitude of true persistence.

claims.statement: In Monte Carlo data generated from the canonical income process with true persistence ρ = 0.9 (σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01, zero initial conditions, N = 1000), equally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences using periods t = [1–30] returns an average estimated persistence of 0.7971.

treatment.label: Equally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences, periods t = [1–30], N = 1000, zero initial conditions, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01

definition.value: the estimation design under study: the grid-search minimum-distance estimator of Blundell et al. (2015) applied to the autocovariance moments of quasidifferences ỹ_it = y_it − ρ y_it−1, with equal weighting of the autocovariance moments; applied to 100 panels simulated from equation (1) with true persistence ρ = 0.9, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01 and zero initial conditions

timing.value: estimation uses the simulated observations for periods t = [1–30] of each panel; the data-generating parameters are fixed before simulation

outcome.label: Estimated persistence of long-lasting shocks, ρ̂

definition.value: the grid value of the persistence ρ (piecewise-linear grid of 100 points from 0.3 to 1.4) that minimises the weighted distance between the data and the theoretical quasidifference autocovariance moments of equations (7)–(9), averaged over the 100 simulated samples of the design; the parentheses report the standard error

timing.value: computed from periods t = [1–30] of each simulated panel

units.value: persistence of long-lasting shocks, ρ (unitless autoregressive coefficient)

magnitude.interpretation: a sizeable downward bias in the estimated persistence that equals about 0.10

estimand.target_population: the persistence parameter of the simulated data-generating process; the estimate is an average across 100 simulated samples of this design

population.description: 100 simulated balanced panels of 1000 individuals each, generated from the canonical income process of equation (1) with true persistence ρ = 0.9, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01 and zero initial conditions; estimation uses periods t = [1–30]
subgroups_defined: equal vs optimal vs diagonal weighting
population.selection: balanced panel by construction; all simulated individuals are retained

identification.source_of_variation: designed Monte Carlo variation: the authors set the true persistence, the variances of fixed effects and of persistent and transitory shocks, the number of individuals, the number of periods, the initial conditions and the weighting scheme, and compare the resulting estimate with the known truth

key_assumptions.assumption: The data are generated by the canonical income process of equation (1), so the true persistence is known by construction and the bias of the estimator can be measured directly.
All shocks and the fixed effect are i.i.d. and orthogonal to each other.

formal.as_written: ηi,t ∼ iid(0, σ²η)   εi,t ∼ iid(0, σ²ε)   αi ∼ iid(0, σ²α)

key_assumptions.assumption: The initial condition of the persistent component is zero for every individual, z_i0 = 0.

The 100-point piecewise-linear grid for the persistence, ranging from 0.3 to 1.4, contains the minimiser of the minimum-distance objective; allowing grid values above one avoids a truncation-induced downward bias.
One hundred simulated samples per design are enough for the average estimate across samples to characterise the estimator's bias.
Once the persistence is fixed, the quasidifference autocovariance moments of equations (7)–(9) identify the variance of fixed effects and the variances of persistent and transitory shocks.

threats_discussed: two local minima of the minimum-distance objective, one near the true persistence and one above one, when the variance of the persistent component in the first sample year is high (Section 4.5)
small-sample bias of GMM estimates of the persistence when the persistence is close to one (Section 2.2, citing Gouriéroux et al. (2010) and Chen et al. (2019))
a downward bias in the average estimated persistence induced by truncating the persistence grid at one (footnote 8)
robustness_checks: heavy-tailed shock distributions, with similar results (footnote 7)
an MA(1) transitory component instead of a purely transitory shock, with similar results (footnote 12)
an intermediate true persistence of 0.95, simulated but not tabulated (footnote 6)
the debiased estimator of Chen et al. (2019) based on splitting the sample, which did not work and is not reported (footnote 16)
unresolved_confounders: the authors state that after some experimentation they could not come up with a robust method for correcting the biases outside the equally weighted case with a high variance of persistent shocks

estimator.value: equally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences (EWMD), with the persistence chosen on a 100-point grid

estimation.specification: minimum distance between the data and model autocovariance moments of quasidifferences (equations (7)–(9)), minimised over a 100-point grid for ρ; the grid value with the lowest objective is the estimate
estimation.weights: equal weighting of the autocovariance moments

sample_n.value: 100 simulated samples, each a balanced panel of N = 1000 individuals

source_table.value: Table 1, Panel A, row (1), column (1)

heterogeneity.dimension: ratio of the variance of transitory to persistent shocks

claims.statement: In Monte Carlo data generated from the canonical income process with true persistence ρ = 0.9 (σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01, nonzero initial conditions, N = 10,000), diagonally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences using periods t = [1–15] returns an average estimated persistence of 1.0216.

treatment.label: Diagonally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences, periods t = [1–15], N = 10,000, nonzero initial conditions, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01

definition.value: the estimation design under study: the grid-search minimum-distance estimator of Blundell et al. (2015) applied to the autocovariance moments of quasidifferences ỹ_it = y_it − ρ y_it−1, with diagonal weighting of the moments (diagonal elements of the inverse of the variance-covariance matrix of the data moments, zero off-diagonal elements); applied to 100 panels simulated from equation (1) with true persistence ρ = 0.9, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01 and nonzero initial conditions

timing.value: estimation uses the simulated observations for periods t = [1–15] of each panel; the data-generating parameters are fixed before simulation

outcome.label: Estimated persistence of long-lasting shocks, ρ̂

timing.value: computed from periods t = [1–15] of each simulated panel

units.value: persistence of long-lasting shocks, ρ (unitless autoregressive coefficient)

magnitude.interpretation: a substantial upward bias in the persistence when the true persistence is low, also in large samples

estimand.target_population: the persistence parameter of the simulated data-generating process; the estimate is an average across 100 simulated samples of this design

population.description: 100 simulated balanced panels of 10,000 individuals each, generated from the canonical income process of equation (1) with true persistence ρ = 0.9, σ²_α = 0.10, σ²_ε = 0.04, σ²_η = 0.01 and nonzero initial conditions; estimation uses periods t = [1–15]
subgroups_defined: equal vs optimal vs diagonal weighting
population.selection: balanced panel by construction; all simulated individuals are retained

identification.source_of_variation: designed Monte Carlo variation: the authors set the true persistence, the variances of fixed effects and of persistent and transitory shocks, the number of individuals, the number of periods, the initial conditions and the weighting scheme, and compare the resulting estimate with the known truth

key_assumptions.assumption: The variance of the persistent component in period zero equals σ²_η(1 − ρ³⁰)/(1 − ρ²), so that income variance in the first sample year matches that of the zero-initial-conditions design observed from period 16.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 100-point piecewise-linear grid for the persistence, ranging from 0.3 to 1.4, contains the minimiser of the minimum-distance objective; allowing grid values above one avoids a truncation-induced downward bias.

claims.statement: Estimated on Danish administrative earnings of the 1952 male cohort, optimally weighted minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences puts the persistence of long-lasting shocks at 0.975.

treatment.label: Optimal weighting of the moments (weight matrix = inverse of the variance-covariance matrix of the data moments) of the autocovariance moments in minimum-distance estimation in quasidifferences on Danish administrative earnings

timing.value: estimated from the 26 annual earnings observations, 1981–2006

units.value: persistence of long-lasting shocks, ρ (unitless autoregressive coefficient)

magnitude.interpretation: estimated at 0.975, close to an estimate in Daly et al. (2022) for their balanced sample

estimand.target_population: the persistence of long-lasting earnings shocks for Danish males born in 1952

population.description: Danish males born in 1952 with administrative earnings records, a balanced panel of 13,543 individuals with 26 annual earnings observations, after the Daly et al. (2022) sample selection
population.birth_cohorts: born in 1952
subgroups_defined: full sample vs 100 bootstrap samples of 1000 individuals
population.selection: ever self-employed individuals dropped; records for males working less than 10% of the year as full-time employees dropped; earnings histories with growth outliers (an increase in adjacent periods by more than 500% or a drop by less than −80%) dropped; balanced panel

identification.source_of_variation: no exogenous variation is used: the income-process parameters are recovered from the autocovariance structure of residual log earnings of a single birth cohort

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings of the Danish cohort follow the canonical income process of equation (1), extended to an MA(1) transitory component and to variances of persistent and transitory shocks that vary over time.
Predictable variation in earnings is fully removed by year-by-year cross-sectional regressions of log earnings on educational dummies, a third-order polynomial in age and the interaction of the two.
Conditioning on a balanced panel and on the Daly et al. (2022) employment and outlier filters does not distort the estimated autocovariance moments.
The weight matrix (optimal, diagonal or equal) used in the minimum-distance criterion is accurate enough in this sample for the selected grid value of the persistence to be meaningful.
The 100-point piecewise-linear grid for the persistence, ranging from 0.3 to 1.4, contains the minimiser of the minimum-distance objective.

population.ages: households aged 30–65 within the 1978–1992 window; on average 36.5 years of age in the first simulated year

identification.source_of_variation: data simulated from a calibrated standard incomplete-markets lifecycle model whose true parameters are known by construction

key_assumptions.assumption: The data are generated by the canonical income process of equation (1), so the true persistence is known by construction and the bias of the estimator can be measured directly.
All shocks and the fixed effect are i.i.d. and orthogonal to each other.

formal.as_written: ηi,t ∼ iid(0, σ²η)   εi,t ∼ iid(0, σ²ε)   αi ∼ iid(0, σ²α)

key_assumptions.assumption: The 100-point piecewise-linear grid for the persistence, ranging from 0.3 to 1.4, contains the minimiser of the minimum-distance objective; allowing grid values above one avoids a truncation-induced downward bias.
One hundred simulated samples per design are enough for the average estimate across samples to characterise the estimator's bias.
Once the persistence is fixed, the quasidifference autocovariance moments of equations (7)–(9) identify the variance of fixed effects and the variances of persistent and transitory shocks.

Income and consumption are generated by a calibrated standard incomplete-markets lifecycle model with zero borrowing constraints, CRRA utility with γ = 2, a 4% real interest rate, work from age 26 to retirement at 65, death at 90, a 0.70 replacement rate, and a discount factor calibrated to a wealth-to-income ratio of 3.

Households are drawn at random from a large simulated dataset and are observed for fifteen years with the PSID 1978–1992 age distribution, so the estimation sample mixes birth cohorts that have already accumulated persistent shocks.

threats_discussed: two local minima of the minimum-distance objective, one near the true persistence and one above one, when the variance of the persistent component in the first sample year is high (Section 4.5)
small-sample bias of GMM estimates of the persistence when the persistence is close to one (Section 2.2, citing Gouriéroux et al. (2010) and Chen et al. (2019))
a downward bias in the average estimated persistence induced by truncating the persistence grid at one (footnote 8)
robustness_checks: heavy-tailed shock distributions, with similar results (footnote 7)
an MA(1) transitory component instead of a purely transitory shock, with similar results (footnote 12)
